definition.text: A government policy that puts a money cost on greenhouse gas emissions so that polluters burn less fossil fuel.

facts.text: A carbon price usually takes the form of a carbon tax or an emissions trading scheme in which firms must buy allowances to emit.
It tackles the problem that greenhouse gas emissions are a negative externality: a harm that no market charges for.
Many economists consider it the most economically efficient way to cut emissions, because it fixes the unpriced external cost at its source.
Carbon pricing covered 28% of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025, and in 2020 it raised $53B in revenue.
Of 21 carbon pricing schemes evaluated, at least 17 reduced emissions, by between 5% and 21%.
About one third of schemes price carbon below $10/tCO2 and most below $40; only Sweden and Switzerland exceed $100/tCO2.
The IPCC says prices of $135–$5500 per tonne in 2030 and $245–$13,000 in 2050 would be needed to stay below the 1.5°C limit.
A 2020 study found that carbon prices have not harmed economic growth in wealthy industrialized democracies.

title: Carbon tax versus emissions trading
article: Carbon price#Carbon tax versus emissions trade

definition.text: The policy choice between a carbon tax, which fixes the price of each tonne emitted, and emissions trading, which fixes the total amount emitted and lets the price adjust.

facts.text: A carbon tax is generally favoured for its simplicity and price stability, while cap-and-trade can in principle hold emissions to a remaining carbon budget.
A tax is easier to enforce broadly; British Columbia enacted and implemented its carbon tax in five months.
Industries may lobby their way out of a carbon tax, while freely handed-out permits can invite corrupt behaviour.
Most cap-and-trade programmes lower the cap by a fixed percentage each year, guaranteeing that emissions decline; permits suit cases where emissions certainty is needed.
Both instruments are efficient and have the same social cost and effect on profits if permits are auctioned.
Prices under a cap are more volatile, which makes them riskier for investors, consumers and governments that auction permits.
Some economists say a cap stops other policies such as renewable subsidies from cutting emissions further; others say only an enforced cap guarantees cuts.

contested_note: Economists disagree over whether a tax or a cap is the better way to price carbon.

definition.text: The choices governments make about how to spend the money raised by a carbon tax or by selling emission permits.

facts.text: One standard proposal returns the money to the public per person; richer people with bigger carbon footprints pay more, and poorer people can come out ahead.
Other proposals fund renewable energy subsidies, research, public transport and car sharing.
Revenue could also subsidise negative emissions, which cost about $150–165 per ton of CO2 depending on the technology.
Per-person refunds would not cover commuters in rural areas or people in poorly insulated houses.

title: Overlapping policies under an emissions cap
article: Carbon price#Interactions with renewable energy policies

definition.text: The way a carbon tax or an emissions cap changes what other climate policies, such as renewable energy subsidies, can achieve.

facts.text: Under a carbon tax, subsidies for renewable energy add to the emission cuts.
Under a binding cap, renewable subsidies bring no further emission cuts while the cap applies.

definition.text: A carbon price that a company sets on its own greenhouse gas emissions, voluntarily and on top of any price a government imposes.

facts.text: As of 2024, 1,753 companies in 56 countries reported using an internal carbon price through the Carbon Disclosure Project.
Tools include internal emissions trading, proxy prices, carbon fees, implicit prices and hybrids of these.
Proxy pricing, used by about two-thirds of reporting companies, puts a set carbon price into investment decisions without any actual payment.
Companies often base their price on the social cost of carbon or on the marginal abatement cost of reaching a target.
An analysis of 500 firms reporting from 2011 to 2018 linked adoption to a significant fall in emissions per unit of revenue and per employee.
Some researchers worry it can serve as greenwashing that deters governments from stricter carbon rules.
It works like a Pigouvian tax inside the firm, making fossil fuel use more expensive.
As of 2024, 1,753 companies across 56 countries reported using it through the Carbon Disclosure Project.

definition.text: Emissions trading applied to carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases: a market with a limited number of allowances to emit, created to limit climate change.

facts.text: A total limit on all participants' emissions sets the price; a polluter emitting more than its quota must buy the right from emitters with fewer emissions.
It works by creating property rights to the atmosphere, a global public good, to deal with an international externality.
Compliance is checked by comparing each emitter's actual emissions with the permits it surrenders.
Countries use it to meet their Paris Agreement pledges, with schemes running in China, the European Union and elsewhere.
In September 2021 allowance prices ranged from €7 per tonne in China's national scheme to €63 per tonne in the EU ETS.
In 2023 the global carbon market was worth a record 881 billion euros, about 87% of it in the EU ETS.
Schemes are usually not matched to the carbon budgets needed for 1.5 °C or 2 °C, and oversupply can push allowance prices too low to matter.

definition.text: How a trading scheme hands out its permits: either free to existing emitters or sold at auction.

facts.text: Under free allocation the government earns no carbon revenue; under auctioning it receives the full value of the permits on average.
Either way the permits are equally scarce, so they sell at the same market price.
Emitters generally profit from permits given to them free, while paying for them reduces their profits.
Advance notice or a gradual introduction keeps the one-time cost of a new carbon price small.

definition.text: Giving out emission permits for free according to how much each firm emitted in the past.

facts.text: It can create perverse incentives, such as a firm that cuts emissions sharply receiving fewer permits later.
Firms that get free permits still raise prices to customers, so permits they did not need become windfall profits.
The EU ETS gives free permits to industries judged exposed to international competition.
Free allocation is complex and encourages rent-seeking and lobbying of governments.

definition.text: Selling emission permits to firms at auction, so that the government receives their value.

facts.text: Businesses tend to oppose auctioning, while economists almost uniformly recommend it.
Auction revenue can fund low-carbon investment and cuts in distortionary taxes.
Auctioning can be more efficient and equitable than free allocation and removes grandfathering's perverse incentive.

definition.text: The risk that a regulator issues too many emission permits, pushing their price so low that firms have little reason to cut emissions.

facts.text: Issuing too few permits has the opposite risk: an excessively high permit price.
The EU ETS price was fairly strong from 2005 to 2009 but was later undermined by oversupply and the Great Recession.
Under the Kyoto Protocol, Russia held surplus allowances after its economic collapse; buying them would not have reduced emissions.

title: Criticisms of carbon trading

definition.text: The arguments that carbon emissions trading is ineffective, unfair or open to abuse.

facts.text: Critics argue climate change needs more radical, systemic cuts in fossil fuel use than pollution trading can deliver.
Carbon trading has been called a form of colonialism that lets rich countries keep consuming while claiming savings abroad.
The market picks the easiest short-term carbon savings, which may differ from the steps needed to reduce climate change.
Some companies in China and India produced greenhouse gases artificially in order to earn credits for destroying them.
Schemes have been criticised for creating speculative markets through financial derivatives, and for changes linked to money laundering.

contested_note: Supporters see carbon trading as an efficient climate tool, while critics call it ineffective, unjust and open to manipulation.

title: Carbon trading and environmental justice
article: Carbon emission trading#Relevance to climate justice

definition.text: The question of whether carbon trading helps poorer countries and communities or leaves them bearing more of the pollution.

facts.text: Trading can move money from richer, higher-emitting countries to poorer, lower-emitting ones for climate action.
Because schemes cap only greenhouse gases, factories can buy permits instead of cutting local air pollution.
Low-income and minority communities living near emitters therefore keep facing an exposure gap.

contested_note: Sources say carbon trading can advance climate justice but has also been linked to environmental injustice near emitters.

title: Global carbon market
article: Carbon emission trading#Potential global carbon market

definition.text: A proposed worldwide market in emission allowances, for which the Paris Agreement provides a legal basis.

facts.text: In 2023 the global value of carbon markets was $948.75 billion, expected to reach 2.68 trillion dollars by 2028.
The Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets, formed at COP 30, plans a global cap near current emissions that falls to net zero by 2050.
Such a market could speed emission cuts seven-fold in participating countries while raising $200 billion per year for clean energy and social programmes.

title: Carbon leakage

definition.text: A rise in greenhouse gas emissions in one country caused by another country cutting its own emissions under stricter climate policies.

facts.text: The leakage rate is the rise in emissions outside the acting countries divided by the cut inside them, as a percentage that can exceed 100%.
A rate above 100% would mean domestic action actually increased global emissions.
Leakage happens when climate policy raises local costs, so production moves to countries with laxer rules while demand stays the same.
It can also happen through fuel markets: lower demand cuts fuel prices, and countries without a carbon price use more.
Estimates for action under the Kyoto Protocol ranged from 5 to 20%, but were seen as very uncertain; there is no consensus on long-term leakage.
The EU gives free ETS allowances to sectors at high risk of leakage, such as aluminium, using a Carbon Leakage Indicator of trade intensity times emission intensity.
Firm-level evidence found the EU ETS cut regulated manufacturers' CO₂ emissions by 14–16% with no observed carbon leakage.
It happens when regulating emissions in one place pushes them to places with less regulation.

contested_note: Sources say there is no consensus on how large long-term carbon leakage is.

definition.text: A market-based way of controlling pollution in which a government caps total emissions and issues permits that polluters can buy and sell.

facts.text: Also called cap and trade, it is used for carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases as well as sulfur dioxide and other pollutants.
Polluters must hold permits equal to their emissions; one that wants to emit more must buy permits from others willing to sell.
In effect the buyer pays a charge for polluting, while the seller is rewarded for cutting its emissions.
Its goal is to meet a set emissions target at the lowest cost, letting firms decide how to meet it, unlike command-and-control rules.
Some schemes let participants bank allowances for later periods, which lets them cut emissions when it is most efficient.
Usually the government lowers the overall limit over time towards a national reduction target.
A 2024 meta-analysis of 80 evaluations across 21 carbon-pricing systems found average emission cuts of about 5–21% (around 4–15% after correcting for publication bias).

definition.text: The idea that trading permits makes pollution cuts happen first wherever they are cheapest, so a target is met at the lowest total cost.

facts.text: Each polluter chooses between buying or selling permits, installing cleaner technology or cutting output, depending on its marginal abatement cost and the permit price.
In theory this spreads reductions efficiently among polluters and lowers compliance costs compared with command-and-control rules.
In a Lagrange optimization of the least-cost target, the Lagrange multiplier plays the role of the market permit price.
This is a version of the equi-marginal principle used in economics to find the most efficient decision.
Coase (1960) argued social costs could be handled by negotiating property rights, assuming perfect markets and equal bargaining power.

definition.text: The development of cap and trade from computer studies of air pollution costs in the late 1960s to national and global carbon markets.

facts.text: Simulation studies between 1967 and 1970 found that a least-cost solution was dramatically cheaper than conventional abatement strategies.
The 1977 Clean Air Act took up an offset mechanism: a firm could emit more if it paid another firm to cut the same pollutant.
The first cap-and-trade system was the US Acid Rain Program under the 1990 Clean Air Act, announced as a paradigm shift in environmental policy.
The approach then spread from US clean air policy to global climate policy and the European Union.

title: Safety valve (emissions trading)
article: Emissions trading#Prices versus quantities, and the safety valve

definition.text: A hybrid of a cap and a tax: a cap-and-trade system in which the permit price is held below a maximum, or above a minimum.

facts.text: Emitters can buy permits on the market or from the government at a set trigger price.
Setting the trigger price high enough, or the permits few enough, lets it mimic a pure quantity or pure price instrument.
A price ceiling removes the certainty of a fixed emissions limit.
A price floor gives certainty for investment in cutting emissions, which matters when cuts are urgent.

definition.text: A trading scheme in which polluters earn credits, or offsets, by cutting emissions below a baseline, often their historical emissions.

facts.text: The credits can be bought by polluters that face a regulatory limit.
Credit programmes usually require additionality: cutting more than existing rules already demand.
Additionality is hard to define and monitor; some companies deliberately raised emissions in order to be paid to remove them.

definition.text: Separate cap-and-trade systems joined together by recognising each other's allowances for compliance.

facts.text: Linking makes a larger carbon market, which can lower compliance costs, raise liquidity and stabilise prices.
Some scholars see linking as a bottom-up starting point for international climate policy.
California and Québec linked their systems in 2014; the EU ETS has linked with Switzerland's system.

definition.text: Markets in licences that give the right to raise pollution at a given location by no more than a set amount, rather than the right to emit a set amount.

facts.text: Pollution at each location is modelled as a linear combination of emissions through a diffusion matrix H, with q=H⋅e.
A polluter that affects several monitoring points must hold a portfolio of licences covering all of them.
Montgomery showed both markets allocate licences efficiently, but pollution-licence markets apply more widely.

title: EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism

definition.text: A European Union carbon tariff on carbon-intensive imports such as steel, cement and some electricity.

facts.text: Its main aim is to stop carbon leakage by charging covered imports the same carbon price as EU producers pay under the EU ETS.
Importers must buy CBAM certificates, priced in line with EU ETS allowances, to cover the emissions embedded in their goods.
It covers aluminium, cement, electricity, fertilisers, hydrogen and iron and steel, with reporting from October 2023 and payment from 2026.
Free EU ETS allowances in the covered sectors will be phased out by 2034.
It may push other countries to adopt carbon pricing; Brazil, Indonesia, Taiwan, Vietnam, Malaysia and Serbia are doing so partly because of it.
Some see it as the start of a climate club of the kind William Nordhaus proposed.
An Asian Development Bank report says it will cut emissions only a little while harming imports to the EU.
Questions remain over its compatibility with WTO rules and its effect on least developed countries.

contested_note: Supporters call it a key fix for carbon leakage, while critics say it does little for emissions, burdens EU firms and may clash with trade rules.

title: Acid Rain Program

definition.text: A US Environmental Protection Agency emissions trading programme that cut sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, the gases that cause acid rain, from power plants.

facts.text: Title IV of the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments set a falling cap on SO2, aiming to bring emissions to 50% of 1980 levels.
It was the first cap-and-trade emissions programme in the United States and became a model for later greenhouse gas schemes.
Plants need an allowance for each ton of SO2 and pay a fine of $2,000 for each ton emitted beyond the allowances they hold.
In 2007 total SO2 emissions were 8.9 million tons, reaching the long-term goal ahead of the 2010 deadline.
The EPA expected compliance costs of $1 billion to $2 billion a year by 2010, only one fourth of what was first predicted.
A 2021 study found it caused lasting air quality gains, cutting mortality risk by 5% over 10 years.
Early over-allocation in Phase I let sources bank allowances, which they drew down in Phase II.
Critics note it cut SO2 by 40%, less than the more than 70% achieved by conventional regulation in the European Union.

contested_note: The EPA, industry and economists call it a success, while sceptical environmentalists argue the cuts came from broader trends and other regulation.

title: Cap and dividend

definition.text: A cap-and-trade system in which all permits are sold and the money is paid back to citizens to offset higher energy prices.

facts.text: A cap is placed on greenhouse gases, often on upstream sources such as fossil fuel suppliers, and they must buy permits for their emissions.
Unlike cap and trade, no permits are given away free; the pollution rents are captured publicly rather than becoming private assets.
Households that emit least receive a bigger dividend than they pay in higher prices, rewarding those who conserve.
The idea was first proposed by Peter Barnes as "Skytrust" in his 2001 book Who Owns the Sky?.
A 2009 US bill would have auctioned 100 percent of permits and returned all proceeds as a monthly dividend, but it did not pass.

contested_note: The policy was vigorously debated, called 'fatally incomplete' by one critic and hailed by Time magazine.

definition.text: Buying and selling water access entitlements, often called water rights, between willing sellers and buyers.

facts.text: A seller holds water rights beyond its current needs, while a buyer short of water is willing to pay for more.
Economic theory says trading moves water from less to more economically productive uses; urban users can pay up to 10 times more than farmers.
First-in-time prior appropriation rights led to inefficient allocation and less adoption of water-saving technology.
Water is a common-pool resource that behaves like a private good once rights make its use rival and excludable.
Trades can harm or help third parties who are neither buyer nor seller.
Water is not a standard commodity: supply is uncertain and moves through complex systems, and supply swings can leave markets thin.
Schemes exist in the western United States, Chile, South Africa, Australia and elsewhere; some consider Australia's the most sophisticated.
Chile's 1981 Water Code made water rights freely tradable private property, a strongly free-market approach that has been controversial.

definition.text: A tradable Kyoto Protocol unit allowing a country to emit one tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent.

facts.text: Units were issued up to each Annex 1 country's Kyoto emission target for the 2008–2012 commitment period.
Under Article 17, countries below their targets could sell spare units to countries above theirs.
Such trading had to be supplemental to domestic action.

title: CORSIA
article: Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation

definition.text: The Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation, which makes airlines buy carbon credits to offset growth in emissions from international flights.

facts.text: The International Civil Aviation Organization adopted it in October 2016, aiming for carbon-neutral growth from 2020.
It is voluntary from 2021 until 2027, when it becomes compulsory; least developed and small island states are not required to join.
Domestic flights are not included, and it will regulate 25% of aviation's international emissions.
Critics say it won't reduce jet fuel demand, and one hundred organisations rejected it as letting warming pass 1.5 °C.

contested_note: Supporters call it a compromise step forward, while environmental groups argue it will not cut aviation emissions enough.

sources.title: Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation

definition.text: Permanently removing emission allowances or carbon credits from circulation so they can never be sold or used again.

facts.text: Retiring allowances shrinks supply under a cap, which raises their scarcity and price.
The EU's Market Stability Reserve invalidated about 2.5 billion allowances on 1 January 2023, and more than 3 billion by 2026.
In voluntary markets, companies retire credits to offset emissions they cannot yet eliminate; a record 164 million were retired in 2023.
Citizen groups have bought and retired sulfur dioxide allowances in US EPA auctions to cut the supply available to polluters.

definition.text: A carbon credit issued by the Clean Development Mechanism for verified emission cuts made by its projects under the Kyoto Protocol.

facts.text: Each unit equals a cut of one tonne of CO2e, measured against a baseline.
Annex I countries buy them from projects in developing countries, where cuts are cheapest, and can use them to meet their targets.
Between 2001 and 7 September 2012 the CDM issued 1 billion CERs; by 2013, 57% came from destroying HFC-23 or N2O.
Prices fell from $20 a tonne in August 2008 to below $5 by September 2012 amid recession and EU ETS over-allocation.

definition.text: China's national emissions trading system for carbon dioxide, which caps emissions per unit of output rather than in total, and began operating in 2021.

facts.text: China proposed a carbon tax in 2010 but never passed it, setting up an emissions trading scheme in February 2021 instead.
It began with power plants and covers 40% of China's emissions, which is 15% of world emissions; it is the largest scheme of its kind.
In July 2021 permits were handed out free and traded at around RMB 50 per tonne, roughly half the EU ETS price.
Seven pilot markets, starting in Shenzhen on June 18, 2013, preceded it, with compliance rates over 96%.
Studies find it cut carbon emissions by up to 18.2%, cut power sector emissions by 13% in 2013-2020, and delivered about a third of China's air pollution health benefits.
Some researchers found it can reduce GDP or hold back innovation.
By 2027 it is expected to cover all major industrial emitters and move to an absolute cap on emissions for stable sectors.

definition.text: A Kyoto Protocol credit for one tonne of CO2 equivalent cut by a Joint Implementation project.

facts.text: Landfill gas capture is an example: methane has a 100-year global warming potential of 25 compared with carbon dioxide.
Burning one tonne of captured methane yields nearly 3 tonnes of CO2, a saving of 22 ERUs.
ERU prices declined 89 percent in 2012, falling to 15 euro cents in December.

title: European Union Emissions Trading System

definition.text: The European Union's cap-and-trade scheme for greenhouse gases, begun in 2005, in which each allowance permits its holder to emit 1 ton of CO2.

facts.text: It was the first large greenhouse gas trading scheme in the world and operates in 30 countries: the 27 EU states plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway.
As of 2026 it covers around 40% of the EU's emissions; its cap should reach zero by 2039.
Between 2005 and 2023, emissions from covered power plants and factories fell by 47%.
A 2023 study found it cut emissions by 10% between 2005 and 2012 with no significant effect on profits or employment.
Phase I over-allocation drove the carbon price to zero in 2007.
It has been criticised for over-allocation, windfall profits, price volatility and failure to meet its goals.
Auction revenue in 2013 - 2025 exceeded €245 billion, most of it going directly to member states.
It has suffered fraud: hackers stole 28 to 30 million euros of allowances in 2011, and VAT fraud cost Germany about €850 million.

contested_note: Critics say it has failed its goals through over-allocation and windfall profits, while proponents call Phase I a learning phase and point to measured cuts.

title: Market Stability Reserve
article: European Union Emissions Trading System#Reform of the EU-ETS and introduction of the Market Stability Reserve (MSR)

definition.text: An EU ETS mechanism that changes how many permits are auctioned each year according to how many surplus permits are in circulation.

facts.text: It runs on predefined rules with no discretion for the Commission or member states.
Back-loading and the MSR law failed to cut the surplus or lift prices in 2014–2017, when prices stayed below €10/tCO2.
Since 2023, allowances in the reserve above a threshold are permanently invalidated; about 2.5 billion were invalidated on 1 January 2023.

definition.text: A second EU emissions trading system for carbon dioxide from buildings, road transport and other sectors outside the original ETS.

facts.text: It covers emissions upstream: fuel suppliers, not end consumers, must report and pay for them.
Its cap aims for a 42% cut by 2030 compared with 2005, with revenue partly funding a Social Climate Fund for vulnerable groups.
Together the two systems will cover 75% of EU greenhouse gas emissions.
In 2025 its start was delayed to 2028 under pressure from member states worried about inflation and energy affordability.

title: Flexible mechanisms

definition.text: The three Kyoto Protocol tools, emissions trading, the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation, that let countries meet emission targets more cheaply by acting in other countries.

facts.text: They rest on the idea that cutting emissions costs different amounts in different places, but benefits the atmosphere equally wherever it happens.
International emissions trading let parties buy Kyoto units from other countries to help meet their targets.
Kyoto caps required Annex I countries to cut emissions on average 5.2% below 1990 levels over 2008 to 2012.
The main argument for them is cost-effectiveness, separating fairness from the efficiency of cutting emissions cheaply.
Critics feared rich countries would avoid domestic cuts and take up all the cheap reductions in developing countries.
Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement are their successor.

contested_note: Negotiators disagreed over whether flexibility was efficient or let developed countries avoid domestic cuts at developing countries' expense.

definition.text: A tradable certificate proving that a certain amount of electricity, typically one megawatthour, was generated from renewable sources.

facts.text: The certificates represent the environmental value of renewable energy and can be traded separately from the electricity itself.
Countries such as Poland, Sweden, the UK, Italy and Belgium use them as a more market-like alternative to feed-in tariffs.
Buying one only shifts the claim to renewable power; it does not change how much renewable energy is generated.

definition.text: A Kyoto Protocol mechanism letting one developed (Annex I) country invest in an emission-cutting project in another and count the cuts towards its own target.

facts.text: Projects earn Emission Reduction Units, each equal to one tonne of CO2 equivalent, taken from the host country's pool of assigned amount units.
Because credits come from the host's pool, the total of credits among Annex I parties does not change.
It raised fewer concerns about spurious reductions than the CDM, since hosts also have emission commitments.
Russia accounted for about two-thirds of projected savings, which were expected to total around 300 million ERUs by 2012.

title: Market design

definition.text: The branch of economics that sets the rules of exchange, who gets what and by what procedure, to build or repair markets so that they give efficient and fair outcomes.

facts.text: It is closely related to mechanism design and auction theory.
Applications pioneered by Alvin Roth include labour-market matching, organ transplantation and school choice.
Under the revenue equivalence theorem, expected revenue is the same in sealed first-price and second-price auctions with independent private values.
Roth and Shapley won the 2012 Nobel prize for the theory of stable allocations and the practice of market design.

notes: General economics page seeded in this chapter; relevant to designing permit auctions but no sentence ties it to emissions markets directly.

title: Personal carbon trading

definition.text: Proposed schemes that would give each adult an equal share of emission credits within a national carbon budget, to be surrendered when buying fuel or electricity.

facts.text: People who emit more than their allowance would buy credits from those who use less, who would profit.
Research finds it would be progressive, moving money from rich to poor, unlike a carbon tax before revenue is redistributed.
Critics point to complexity, high implementation costs and possible political unacceptability; a 2008 UK study found it ahead of its time.
Norfolk Island trialled the world's first personal carbon trading programme starting in 2011.

contested_note: Proponents call it equitable and effective, while critics and a UK government study call it costly, complex and premature.

definition.text: A land-use tool that lets developers buy the building rights of land in a protected sending area and use them to build more densely in a receiving area.

facts.text: It rests on the idea that land carries a bundle of property rights, including the right to develop.
Sending areas are farmland, wilderness or historic sites at risk of development; receiving areas are urban areas suited to higher density.
Landowners get paid for conserving environmental, heritage or farming values, and sprawl is curbed by concentrating development.
TDR programs operate in over 200 U.S. communities.

title: Monitoring, reporting and verification
article: Emissions trading#Measuring, reporting, verification and enforcement

definition.text: The checks that make an emissions market credible: measuring or calculating emissions, reporting them, and having them verified by government or third-party auditors.

facts.text: Some emissions are measured by sensors in chimneys, but many activities rely on calculations instead.
Polluters exceeding their allowances face fines and sanctions; concerns include the cost of checking and the risk of facilities lying.
Acid Rain Program plants had to monitor SO2 and NOx continuously and send data to the EPA daily.
Robust independent third-party validation and verification is one of the Core Carbon Principles for voluntary credits.

sources.title: Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market

title: Verification and validation

definition.text: Two independent checks: verification asks whether a product or system meets its specifications, validation whether it serves its intended purpose.

facts.text: ISO 14064 sets requirements for bodies that validate and verify greenhouse gas claims.

notes: General quality-management page (medical devices, lab methods); only one sentence touches greenhouse gases. The carbon-market concept is covered by 'Monitoring, reporting and verification'.

definition.text: A carbon offset, also called a Verified Emission Reduction, traded in the voluntary market and usually certified outside the Kyoto Protocol.

facts.text: One VER equals 1 tonne of CO2 emissions.
Companies and individuals buy them to compensate voluntarily for their emissions.
Standards set how reductions are measured, and every VER should at least be verified by an independent third party.

definition.text: Tradable certificates proving that a certain amount of energy saving has been achieved, usually tied to an obligation on energy suppliers to save energy.

facts.text: Suppliers of electricity, gas and oil must deliver efficiency measures equal to a set percentage of their annual sales or pay a penalty.
As with emissions trading, tradability in theory meets the overall saving target at least cost.
Great Britain started a scheme in 2002, Italy in 2005, and France and Denmark a year later.

definition.text: A sudden, usually unexpected addition to income well above the norm, arising from luck or circumstance rather than planning.

facts.text: A windfall profit is the business version, caused for example by unexpected demand or government regulation.
Under the EU ETS, fossil generators priced freely allocated permits into electricity, reaping a massive windfall gain.
Some legislators favour a windfall profits tax, since taxing unforeseen profits should not hurt the company.

definition.text: The problem that a regional pollutant traded under a cap can pile up in some places, since the same amount does far more harm in some locations than others.

facts.text: CO2 has a similar effect wherever it is released, so location does not matter, unlike regional pollutants such as SO2, NOx and mercury.
Because carbon trading limits only greenhouse gases, factories can buy permits without cutting local air pollution, leaving nearby low-income communities exposed.
Markets in location-based pollution licences, which cap the rise in pollution at each monitoring point, are one answer to the problem.

definition.text: A market-based approach, run at watershed scale, in which sources that can cut water pollution cheaply sell pollution-reduction credits to sources for whom cuts are costly.

facts.text: It rests on the fact that different sources in a watershed face very different costs to control the same pollutant.
Most programmes trade nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen.
The US EPA issued its Water Quality Trading Policy in 2003, and all programmes must meet the Clean Water Act.
Funders include watershed beneficiaries, polluters compensating for their impacts and public good payers.

sources.title: United States regulation of point source water pollution
